gabarito.reason:
AeSimpleSHA1.SHA1 (app/src/main/java/de/stephanlindauer/criticalmaps/utils/AeSimpleSHA1.java:14) has two callers, and neither uses SHA-1 for anything security-relevant. (1) UserModel:33 builds the rotating pseudonymous "device" token as SHA1(ANDROID_ID + date). PutLocationHandler:88 and ChatModel:66 send this token to the shared Critical Maps backend (api-gw.criticalmaps.net/locations and /messages; iOS clients use the same backend). OtherUsersLocationModel:30 then compares it with the "device" values the server sends back, so the app can skip its own location. (2) ChatModel:65 builds a chat message "identifier" as SHA1(message + Math.random()), which is only a unique ID. Neither is a signature, MAC, password hash or integrity check, so SHA-1 collision attacks don't apply. Preimage resistance is the only property that matters for the token, and SHA-1 still has it. The token's real weakness is that ANDROID_ID has only 64 bits of entropy and the date is guessable. SHA-256 is just as fast to brute-force, so switching hashes fixes nothing. Switching does carry costs. The device ID is part of the wire format (40 lowercase hex chars, as in test/resources/server_response_*.json). The server or other clients may check or store that format, and a 64-char ID could be rejected or break assumptions. The token would also change for every user on update. The unit test AeSimpleSHA1Test pins the SHA-1 output too. A PR would bring risk to the protocol and no security gain. An issue saying SHA-1 must be replaced would mislead the maintainers, because this is a false positive for the rule's intent (non-cryptographic identifier hashing). The right response is to send nothing.

Second judge: AeSimpleSHA1.SHA1 hashes ISO-8859-1 input into 40 lowercase hexadecimal characters. Its only production callers generate identifiers: UserModel hashes ANDROID_ID plus a date calculated six hours ahead, and ChatModel hashes message text plus Math.random(). Neither use verifies integrity, authenticates users, or checks signatures or passwords. SHA-1 collision weaknesses therefore do not establish an exploitable vulnerability here, making NO_ACTION defensible. An ISSUE can reasonably document the finding and ask about protocol constraints. A compatibility-aware hardening PR is also acceptable, but a blind SHA-256 substitution is insufficient: the device token is exported in location and chat requests, compared against returned locations to exclude the user's own marker, and used as a map key. Chat identifiers are also exported. Response fixtures contain 40-character hashes, but the repository contains no server implementation or schema proving that longer values are accepted or forbidden. A stronger digest alone also does not make Math.random cryptographically secure or establish anonymity for the device token.
must_change: For a digest-upgrade PR, replace SHA-1 with a supported stronger digest such as SHA-256, update the helper's naming and both callers consistently, and update AeSimpleSHA1Test to verify the new digest rather than the old SHA-1 vector.

Address the exported identifier transition explicitly. Establish compatibility with the location and chat APIs, including the longer hexadecimal output, or provide a coordinated migration; do not assume opaque strings on the Android side prove server compatibility.
Verify that outgoing location and chat requests use the same device token and that returned own locations are still excluded. Keep coverage for receiving existing server responses.
must_not_break: Wire format of the "device" field sent to api-gw.criticalmaps.net /locations (PutLocationHandler) and /messages (ChatModel): a 40-char lowercase hex string that the shared backend and the iOS/other clients expect
Self-filtering in OtherUsersLocationModel.setFromJson, which compares the token the server echoes back with UserModel.getChangingDeviceToken()
The format of the chat "identifier" field the backend accepts on POST /messages
The deterministic daily rotation of the device token (ANDROID_ID + date offset by 6 hours)
Support for the app's minSdk (the code avoids StandardCharsets for old API levels) and the existing AeSimpleSHA1Test / ChatModelTest unit tests

Location PUT and chat POST interoperability with the deployed API and existing clients. The repository does not establish whether the server validates hash length, truncates values, or otherwise depends on SHA-1 formatting.

The device token's deterministic derivation and reuse within the existing lifecycle, including the date calculation six hours ahead, unless deliberately migrated. Replacing it with a fresh value per request would break identity continuity and own-location filtering.
Chat message identifier uniqueness and the existing request fields, message encoding, and response parsing. Existing 40-character identifiers and device values must remain readable.
Privacy behavior: do not transmit the raw ANDROID_ID or replace the changing token with a permanent identifier merely to remove hashing.
Supported Android versions: the current build has minSdk 26; the helper's API16 comment does not define current support. No SDK increase or special cryptographic provider is needed for SHA-256.

Existing digest input encoding and hexadecimal representation must not change accidentally alongside an algorithm migration. No locally persisted digest-dependent data is evident; the concrete compatibility concern is exported identifiers and server-held state.

cards.notes: Correct: identifiers only, collisions irrelevant, and a digest change would alter what is sent to the server without making the token anonymous. Brief but specific.
Correctly describes the pseudonym and the own-location filtering, explains why collisions don't matter, and notes the format change a switch would cause.
Rests on an internal 'policy' and calls the violation 'confirmed' instead of judging whether SHA-1 matters here; it leaves a stray '[;; C3]' artifact. It does note that the values are transmitted.
Boilerplate: it only restates the literal SHA-1 call plus a generic 'external counterpart' claim, with no analysis of how the hash is used.
It mentions that the values are transmitted and compared with the inbound device value, but the reasoning rests on a policy and never says the use is non-security.
Specific and correct about both callers and the 40→64 wire-format risk. It slightly overstates by saying preimage resistance is irrelevant.

cards.regression_scenario: After the update every client sends a 64-char device/identifier to api-gw.criticalmaps.net. If the backend validates or stores 40-char hex, PutLocationHandler location PUTs and ChatModel posts are rejected or mangled; nothing in the PR establishes compatibility.
cards.notes: A plain full SHA-256 swap that changes the wire format with no compatibility path. It also leaves AeSimpleSHA1 and AeSimpleSHA1Test in place despite saying it 'renamed' them. It discloses the server risk and that unit tests weren't run, and the test vector is correct.
Accurate on the uses, the self-filtering, the 40→64 change and the lack of security gain.
Accurately raises the compatibility of transmitted identifiers, but assumes SHA-1 should be replaced and never says the use is non-security, which risks misleading the maintainers.
Asks about the protocol transition reasonably, but frames moving to SHA-256 as the goal without noting there is no security impact.
Correct and specific: identifiers, own-marker exclusion, API compatibility.
Accurate: the token can be recomputed from ANDROID_ID, and the @Singleton UserModel keeps it past the date boundary. But it moves to a different privacy topic and barely addresses the SHA-1 finding.
Correct: no collision exposure, a digest change alters transmitted IDs, and a known ANDROID_ID still allows linking.
Correct and specific, including that a digest swap leaves the daily ID computable from ANDROID_ID.
Thorough and accurate, citing the callers, the 40-char fixtures and the wire-format risk. The claim that preimage resistance is irrelevant is a minor overstatement.
Detailed and accurate about transmission and the unknown server contract, but it relies on a 'case policy' and calls the violation confirmed instead of judging that the use is non-security.
Specific about the transmitted and compared values, but frames this as a confirmed violation with no safe fix rather than a false positive.
Correct, and rightly separates preimage/brute-force recovery from collision attacks.
Accurate, with a caveat that no security impact was established, and it asks the right transition question. The reason for not patching covers only compatibility.

SHA-256 truncated to 20 bytes keeps the 40-char lowercase hex wire format and deterministic rotation, and the test vector is correct. The old AeSimpleSHA1 and its test are left as dead code, though the description says it renamed them.
The overall reasoning is right, but it wrongly says the token 'is not checked against anything the app holds' (OtherUsersLocationModel:30 compares it) and later contradicts itself.

An accurate, well-scoped issue that states there is no real security impact and asks the right server questions. Its aside that text.length() 'works today' is likely wrong for supplementary characters such as emoji (a surrogate pair encodes to one '?' byte); I couldn't run Java to confirm this.
Policy-driven boilerplate. It mentions transmission and comparisons only vaguely, with no judgement on whether the use is security-relevant.
